summary.text: It is made of hydrogen and helium, and its banded outer atmosphere has storms such as the Great Red Spot, recorded since 1831.
Its mass is nearly 2.5 times that of all the other planets combined, and at least 115 moons orbit it.

facts.label: Mass versus others
facts.value: Nearly 2.5 times all other planets combined

items.prompt: Jupiter is not a perfect sphere: it is wider at its equator. What causes the bulge?

options.label: Heat swelling its equator
The pull of its four largest moons
Its strong magnetic field pushing outward
Its rapid rotation

items.explain: Because of its rapid rotation, the planet is an oblate spheroid, with an equator radius about 7% larger than at the poles.

items.prompt: Far from the Sun, Jupiter still gives off more heat than it receives from sunlight. Where does the extra come from?

options.label: Hydrogen burning like in a small star
The slow contraction of its interior
Friction from its many moons
Radioactive iron in its core

items.explain: The ongoing contraction of Jupiter's interior generates more heat than the planet receives from the Sun.

items.prompt: Jupiter built a solid core first, then gathered gas. What does that require about timing?

options.label: It formed while gas still filled the young Solar System
It formed after the other planets had cleared the gas
It formed long after the early nebula had dispersed
It formed from gas blown off the young Sun

items.explain: Because it formed a core and then accumulated gas, it must have formed before the solar nebula was fully dispersed.

items.prompt: In the 'grand tack' idea, Jupiter drifted inward early on. What did that do to planets already circling nearer the Sun?

options.label: They were pulled in to become its moons
They were flung out of the Solar System
Their orbits were upset and several collided
Their orbits stayed untouched by the move

items.explain: Jupiter's inward migration upset the orbits of several super-Earths, causing them to collide destructively.

items.prompt: Jupiter is surrounded by a faint system of rings. What are they mainly made of?

options.label: Large chunks of ice
Fine dust
Slabs of solid rock
Frozen clouds of gas

items.explain: The rings of Jupiter consist mainly of dust.

items.prompt: What generates Jupiter's magnetic field, the strongest in the Solar System?

options.label: A solid iron core turning inside it
The solar wind charging its atmosphere
Eddy currents in deep fluid metallic hydrogen
The pull of its four big moons

items.explain: Its field is generated by eddy currents within the fluid, metallic hydrogen core.

paragraphs.heading: The biggest planet
paragraphs.text: Counting outward from the Sun, Jupiter is the fifth planet, and it is the biggest one in the Solar System. It is a gas giant, and a heavy one: nearly two and a half times the mass of all the other planets put together, yet still a little under a thousandth of the Sun's mass. Across, it is 11 times as wide as Earth and a tenth as wide as the Sun. It takes 11.86 years to go once around the Sun, at a distance of 5.20 AU, or 778.5 million kilometres.

paragraphs.heading: A bright light named for a god
paragraphs.text: Apart from the Moon and Venus, nothing natural in our night sky is brighter, and people have watched it since prehistoric times. Both the ancient Greeks and the Romans named it after the chief of their gods: Zeus for the Greeks, Jupiter for the Romans. In 1976 the International Astronomical Union made the name official, and it names newly found moons after the god's lovers, favourites and descendants. The adjective for the planet is Jovian. An older one, jovial, used by astrologers in the Middle Ages, now means happy or merry, moods that astrology ascribed to Jupiter.

paragraphs.heading: Stripes, storms and a squashed shape
paragraphs.text: By mass, its atmosphere is 76 percent hydrogen and 24 percent helium, with traces of carbon, ammonia, water vapour and other substances. The outer layer is split into bands that run parallel to the equator, and where neighbouring bands meet, the air is turbulent and stormy. The most obvious result is the Great Red Spot, a giant storm on record since 1831. The planet spins once every ten hours, so fast that it bulges: its radius at the equator is about 7 percent bigger than at the poles.

paragraphs.heading: Inside the giant
paragraphs.text: Under the clouds, Jupiter is thought to have an outer mantle of fluid metallic hydrogen around a diffuse inner core of denser material. Its magnetic field, made by swirling currents in that fluid metallic hydrogen, is the strongest in the Solar System and its second-largest continuous structure. The solar wind interacts with the planet's magnetosphere and stretches it outward. The interior is still contracting, and that contraction gives off more heat than Jupiter receives from the Sun.

paragraphs.heading: Moons and rings
paragraphs.text: At least 115 moons circle Jupiter. The four largest, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, travel inside the magnetosphere and can be seen with ordinary binoculars; Ganymede is bigger than the planet Mercury. Jupiter also has a faint set of rings made mainly of dust, in three main parts: an inner halo, a fairly bright main ring and an outer gossamer ring. They look reddish in visible and near-infrared light, and their age is unknown.

paragraphs.heading: The first planet to form
paragraphs.text: Jupiter is believed to be the oldest planet, formed just one million years after the Sun and about 50 million years before Earth. Models place its birth at or beyond the snow line, the distance from the early Sun where it was cold enough for water and other volatiles to condense into solids. It built a solid core first and gathered its gas atmosphere afterwards, so it must have formed before the solar nebula had cleared away. Once it passed 50 Earth masses it opened a gap in that nebula, and within 3 to 4 million years it reached its final mass.

paragraphs.heading: A planet that wandered
paragraphs.text: One idea, the grand tack hypothesis, says Jupiter began forming about 3.5 AU from the Sun and then moved inward, as its growing mass interacted with the gas disk around the Sun and with orbital resonances from Saturn. On the way it disturbed several super-Earths orbiting closer in, which collided and destroyed one another. Saturn later moved inward faster until the two were caught in a 3:2 mean motion resonance near 1.5 AU, which reversed their course and carried both out to where they are today. The whole back-and-forth took 3 to 6 million years.
